common_name: Chinese Cling Peach (Historic Clingstone Peach, Foundational Elberta Parent)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break, in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0-6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; Chinese Cling has a relatively low, moderate chill requirement of roughly 450-600 hours, so it sets a reliable crop through most zone 6-9 winters.

directions: Chinese Cling is one of the most historically important peaches in American horticulture, imported from southern China to Charleston, South Carolina around 1850 and quickly distributed through the Southern nursery trade for its large size, vigorous growth, and adaptability to warm climates. It bears large, round, downy-skinned fruit with white, richly flavored, strongly clingstone flesh streaked with red near the pit — a distinctly Old World peach character quite different from the freestone yellow peaches that later came to dominate American orchards. Its greatest legacy is genetic: Samuel Rumph of Marshallville, Georgia crossed Chinese Cling with Early Crawford in 1875 to produce Elberta, the freestone peach that became the backbone of the Southern peach industry for a century, and Chinese Cling parentage runs through many other historic Southern cultivars as well. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart after petal fall, prune annually to an open-vase form, and maintain a preventive fungicide and dormant-oil spray program, since like most heirloom clingstone types it has only modest resistance to brown rot and peach leaf curl.

common_name: Early Crawford Peach (Crawford's Early, Historic 19th-Century Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break, in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0-6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; Early Crawford requires roughly 700-750 chill hours, so it performs best toward the cooler end of zone 5-8 rather than in the mildest zone 9 winters.

directions: Early Crawford, also sold as Crawford's Early, was discovered around 1815-1820 by William Crawford of Middletown, New Jersey, and went on to become one of the most widely planted peaches in 19th-century America, prized for its large, showy, yellow-skinned, red-blushed fruit and rich, yellow, freestone flesh. Its combination of size, color, and flavor made it the commercial standard of its era and the parent stock behind many later cultivars, most notably crossed with Chinese Cling by Samuel Rumph in 1875 to produce Elberta, the freestone peach that eventually eclipsed it in Southern orchards. Trees are vigorous and productive but the fruit buds are only moderately cold-hardy and the ripening fruit is prone to brown rot in humid weather, so growers should thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart after petal fall, prune to an open-vase form for airflow, and maintain a fungicide program through the ripening period. It remains worth growing today chiefly for its historical significance and its rich, old-fashioned peach flavor, which many heirloom fruit growers consider superior to modern shipping-bred cultivars.
